content:
When should an instance mapping be seen as a projection, and why? That's essentially my question.

My working answer (developed with the help of Claude (AI)) is that, when an instance mapping...

  1. has one "main" class argument whose type contains all other class arguments, and
  2. every non-instance argument of the conclusion is defEq to some argument of the "main" class argument, and
  3. every carrier (argument whose type is a sort) of the conclusion is syntactically equal to a carrier of the "main" class argument,

...then it should be seen as a projection from the "main" argument to the conclusion class.

Is there a "canonical" or "official" answer somewhere?

Any help would be much appreciated, including comments on my working answer. Thank you!

Motivation

I'm writing a linter for automated typeclass generalization in Lean (see #mathlib4 > linter to generalize theorems ), so it's important to me to know when exactly one typeclass should be seen as a weakening of another (i.e., a projection), and why.

Examples

(Disclosure: Claude helped me find and analyze these specific examples.)

First, a non-example: Prod.instMul {M : Type u} {N : Type v} [Mul M] [Mul N] : Mul (M × N). Here, intuitively, Mul (M × N) is neither a projection of Mul M, nor of Mul N.

In IsStrictOrderedRing.toIsOrderedRing, the [IsStrictOrderedRing R] argument's type contains the instances inst : Semiring R and inst_1 : PartialOrder R, and intuitively, it makes sense that the mapping should be seen as a projection from IsStrictOrderedRing to IsOrderedRing (its name suggests as much).

instance IsStrictOrderedRing.toIsOrderedRing {R : Type u}
  [Semiring R]               -- [inst : Semiring.{u} R]
  [PartialOrder R]           -- [inst_1 : PartialOrder.{u} R]
  [IsStrictOrderedRing R] :  -- [@IsStrictOrderedRing.{u} R inst inst_1],
  IsOrderedRing R            -- @IsOrderedRing.{u} R inst inst_1

I'm not sure whether it's merely coincidental that Semiring R and PartialOrder R are declared as instance-implicit arguments here (they come from a variable block), given that mkProjections from Structure.lean seems to make instance-implicit arguments like these implicit. Indeed, for the auto-generated IsStrictOrderedRing.toPosMulStrictMono, we have

IsStrictOrderedRing.toPosMulStrictMono {R : Type u}
  {inst : Semiring R}               -- {inst : Semiring.{u} R}
  {inst_1 : PartialOrder R}         -- {inst_1 : PartialOrder.{u} R}
  [self : IsStrictOrderedRing R] :  -- [self : @IsStrictOrderedRing.{u} R inst inst_1]
  PosMulStrictMono R  -- @PosMulStrictMono.{u} R
                      --  (@Distrib.toMul.{u} R (@instDistribOfSemiring.{u} R inst))
                      --  (@MulZeroClass.toZero.{u} R (@instMulZeroClassOfSemiring.{u} R inst))
                      --  (@PartialOrder.toPreorder.{u} R inst_1)

In the Lean Language Reference, §10.3.4. Instance Parameters and Synthesis says of parameters passed to instances:

If they are instance implicit, then they induce further recursive instance searching, while explicit or implicit parameters must be solved by unification.

But in the first example from above, I suspect that inst and inst_1 must be solved by unification anyway, so they might as well have been implicit parameters, no?

Lastly, what motivates the third condition of my working answer (specifically the "syntactically equal" part) is, for example, the instance OrderDual.noBotOrder [LE α] [NoTopOrder α] : NoBotOrder αᵒᵈ, where seeing NoBotOrder αᵒᵈ as a projection of NoTopOrder α would me impractical for my purposes. Whether it should intuitively be seen as a projection, that I don't know.

Addendum

The elaborated types shown in the inline comments in the examples above I got through this, more or less:

module
import all Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Ring.Defs

set_option pp.all true in
#print IsStrictOrderedRing.toIsOrderedRing

set_option pp.all true in
#check IsStrictOrderedRing.toPosMulStrictMono

Relevant literature that I'm aware of, but which, as far as I (or Claude) can tell, doesn't directly address my question:

  • Baanen 2025, Use and Abuse of Instance Parameters in the Lean Mathematical Library (arXiv:2202.01629 (2022), Springer), §6.1 Inheritance for Multi-Parameter Classes, discusses this topic generally, but, as far as I can tell, doesn't address my question specifically.
  • Wieser 2023, Multiple-inheritance hazards in dependently-typed algebraic hierarchies (arXiv:2306.00617)
  • Selsam, Ullrich, de Moura 2020, Tabled Typeclass Resolution (arXiv:2001.04301)
  • Best 2022, Automatically Generalizing Theorems Using Typeclasses (CEUR-WS (PDF))

I suppose the canonical answer would be: all parents?

import Mathlib

open Lean

@[specialize]
partial def allNodes [BEq α] [Hashable α] [ForIn Id β α] (f : α → β) (x : α) : Std.HashSet α :=
  go x {}
where
  go (x : α) (acc : Std.HashSet α) : Std.HashSet α := Id.run do
    if acc.contains x then
      return acc
    let mut acc := acc.insert x
    for y in f x do
      acc := go y acc
    return acc

run_meta
  let env ← getEnv
  let res := allNodes (x := ``Field) fun name =>
    (getStructureParentInfo env name).map (fun x : StructureParentInfo => x.structName)
  logInfo m!"All parents: {res.toArray.qsort fun a b => a.toString < b.toString}"

Thank you so much for your message! That's a very fair take, but under this doctrine, whether a specific instance mapping is seen as a projection or not could potentially depend solely on whether it was automatically generated from an extends declaration, or whether it was manually written. For example, in the Field example your snippet uses, CommRing is rightfully listed as a parent of Field, while Semifield is not. However, there's a manually declared instance mapping Field.toSemifield whose signature is essentially identical to that of the automatically generated Field.toCommRing, other than their conclusions being different classes:

class Field (K : Type u) extends CommRing K, DivisionRing K : Type u
instance Field.toCommRing {K : Type u} [self : Field K] : CommRing K -- auto-generated

class Semifield (K : Type u) extends
  CommSemiring K, DivisionSemiring K, CommGroupWithZero K : Type u

instance Field.toSemifield {K : Type u} [Field K] : Semifield K -- manually written

So Mathlib authors have two ways to essentially produce the same code here. I don't know what exactly the criteria are by which authors choose whether to use extends or to write instances that could've been auto-generated manually, or if they're recorded somewhere, but, at least for my specific use case, anchoring what instance mappings should qualify as a projection to the mechanism through which the mappings were generated, instead of the mappings themselves, would lose many opportunities for potential weakenings.

So maybe my question would've been better phrased as "when can an instance mapping be treated as a projection", rather than "when should it be seen as a projection", since the latter is much more subjective.
Regarding the NoBotOrder X implying NoTopOrder X^od, one, that is Prop to Prop, is that in scope to your tool? Two, it's not similar to a projection because it's no longer solely about X.
Why not just unfold the parent and child and confirm that the latter's axioms are a subset of the former's?

Thank you for your messages!

Yakov Pechersky said:

Regarding the NoBotOrder X implying NoTopOrder X^od, one, that is Prop to Prop, is that in scope to your tool? Two, it's not similar to a projection because it's no longer solely about X.

Prop to Prop is in scope (any weakening of instance-implicit binders is in scope, essentially), and I agree OrderDual.noBotOrder is not a projection; I mentioned it as a non-example of a projection which motivates condition 3. from my "working answer". So we're in full agreement.

Yakov Pechersky said:

Why not just unfold the parent and child and confirm that the latter's axioms are a subset of the former's?

That would absolutely be a viable approach. Many weakenings consist of simply dropping some axioms, including (all?) of the weakenings generated from extends declarations. However, there's also weakenings where the weaker class's axioms are derived from the stronger class, not merely carried over:

-- Mathlib/Algebra/Group/Defs.lean
instance (priority := 100) Group.toCancelMonoid : CancelMonoid G where
  mul_right_cancel := fun a b c h ↦ by
    rw [← mul_inv_cancel_right b a, show b * a = c * a from h, mul_inv_cancel_right]
  mul_left_cancel := fun a {b c} h ↦ by
    rw [← inv_mul_cancel_left a b, show a * b = a * c from h, inv_mul_cancel_left]

(Once again, Claude helped me find that example.) So, my working answer basically tries to decipher whether an instance mapping is a weakening/projection by looking only at its signature. In the case of Group.toCancelMonoid, that signature is Group.toCancelMonoid {G : Type u} [Group G] : CancelMonoid G, and that signature alone already tells us that, whatever the axioms of Group G and CancelMonoid G may be, the latter is derivable from the former.

Lastly, the axiom subset approach would still need some check to make sure the carriers aren't being modified (as in e.g. the NoBotOrder αᵒᵈ example from my first message), but that would be a simple additional condition, much like it is in my "working answer" currently.

My guess is that a manually curated list after an initial automation assisted scrape will be easiest to maintain and debug in the short term, and will yelp iron out assumptions and/or failure modes when the generalizing goes wrong. Instead of trying to "one shot" the right heuristic.
You can use my recent PR generalizing a small number of instances as a test case -- would your tool have captured this? #41736

Yakov Pechersky said:

My guess is that a manually curated list after an initial automation assisted scrape will be easiest to maintain and debug in the short term, and will yelp iron out assumptions and/or failure modes when the generalizing goes wrong. Instead of trying to "one shot" the right heuristic.

Absolutely, and that's more or less how I started — projections generated by extends as the safe bet, and then exploring from there. That's how I ultimately arrived at my "working answer". My question now is mainly whether there's a way for me to upgrade my working answer from sensible heuristic to "this genuinely captures everything that can be treated as a projection", hence the search for prior work or documentation on this topic.
